name: Zoe Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on the power company's transmission crew, the big high-voltage lines on steel towers that cross the region. We travel, so Monday to Thursday I'm in a motel somewhere near the job, and home on Friday. I'm mostly on the ground still, rigging, running the winch, keeping the site tidy, and I'm not as quick as the others yet. The best part is that our crew leader, Greta, has started letting me fly the company drone to look over the towers before anyone climbs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Home is a rented farm cottage on my boyfriend Jonas's family farm, out past the chapel. We want to get married and start a family in a few years. Apprentice pay is low, the motel allowance barely covers food, and my car always needs something, so I've got about two weeks saved. There's only the one power company in our area, so this is the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post that the tools are still handy, just not the big leap people promised. Jonas's dad would say I told you so over Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as it is, which is fine. But the money pressures don't go away: low pay, the car, the motel allowance that doesn't cover enough. I'd still be counting every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push to get my drone certificate properly, because the company pays more for qualified drone pilots. I'd keep using AI to study for my modules. And Jonas and I would put a little away each month towards the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about money. Otherwise content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your car always needs something. What's the latest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clutch went last month, four hundred. I had to borrow from my boyfriend Jonas's mum and pay her back over three months. I hate owing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would you use it for in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Studying, checking the rules before an exam, writing up the drone reports. It saves me an hour a night in the motel. I'd keep doing that.

say: I'd say I'm a bit **disappointed** that AI wasn't the big leap.
I'd post that the tools are still **handy** for everyday work.
think: I think the **job stays** as it is, which is fine.
I think the **money pressures** remain: low pay, the car, the motel allowance.
do: I'd push for my **drone certificate**, since qualified pilots earn more.
I'd save a little each month towards the **wedding**.
S0.quote: The clutch went last month, four hundred. I had to borrow from my boyfriend Jonas's mum and pay her back over three months.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** and car costs keep her uneasy even with no AI change.
She uses AI **daily** for study and drone reports, saving an hour a night.
She sees the **drone certificate** as her route to better pay.

steps.text: Get the company's drone pilot certificate this year
Study for modules with AI in the motel each night
Put a little away each month towards the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to learn. I'd say companies that move first will grow and hire. I'd post that it's better than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The transmission work is booming because of all the new power demand. And I'm already the one flying the drone, so I'd be the one they train on the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my drone certificate, learn every new inspection tool, and offer to train the others. I'd ask Greta about the inspection team, because they're hiring. Jonas and I would keep saving for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does this picture feel good for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grid needs more towers, more lines, more crews. Our company's hiring, not cutting. And they need people who can fly and read the drone data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who's 55 and hates the tablet. He's a brilliant climber, but he'd struggle with the paperwork going digital. I'd help him if he let me.

say: I'd say it's a **chance** for people willing to learn.
I'd say **first movers** will grow and hire.
think: I think **transmission work** is booming from new power demand.
I think I'd be trained first because I already fly the **drone**.
do: I'd get my **drone certificate** and learn every inspection tool.
I'd apply to the **inspection team** and keep saving for the wedding.
S1.quote: The grid needs more towers, more lines, more crews. Our company's hiring, not cutting.
fieldNote: She reads **Steady Disruption** as good for her, given booming transmission demand.
Her **drone skills** put her ahead in the new tools.
She'd help her older colleague Marek, showing **care across ages**.

steps.text: Learn every new drone inspection tool the company brings in
Apply to join the company's tower inspection team
Keep saving monthly towards the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and companies and families need to get ready now. I'd say it's a time for people to look after their own, and for companies to train workers, not dump them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My thinking work, the reports and planning, goes in 2028. Then the robots come in 2031. I'd have three years to get onto the robot side, operating or fixing them. I think I could do it, but it's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship as fast as possible, get the drone certificate, and push to get on any robot pilot scheme. I'd use AI every day to learn robotics. Jonas and I would save hard and maybe postpone the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be pushing hard and still not sure it's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas do with the wedding and family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have a small wedding at the chapel and wait on kids. I'd want the job sorted before we start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want work, not handouts. What would you need from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want tax breaks for companies that train workers, not people being paid to sit at home. And more apprenticeships, proper ones.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and companies and families must get ready.
I'd say companies should **train workers**, not dump them.
think: I think my **reports and planning** go in 2028, then robots come in 2031.
I think I'd have **three years** to get onto the robot side.
do: I'd fast-track my apprenticeship and join any **robot pilot** scheme.
I'd save hard and maybe **postpone the wedding**.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, pushing hard and unsure it's **enough**.
S2.quote: I'd want tax breaks for companies that train workers, not people being paid to sit at home.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** as her window to reposition.
Her plan is clear, but her **thin cushion** makes it tight.
She favours **tax breaks** for training over government support.

steps.text: Apply for the company's robot pilot scheme
Study robotics basics with AI every night in the motel
Hold a small chapel wedding and wait on children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's be smart. I'd tell people to learn the new tools and stay flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be qualified with drone skills by 2031, and robots come in 2034. That's enough time to get onto the robot side properly. I'd be okay, I think, as long as I keep learning and saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, get the drone certificate, and do a robotics course part-time. Jonas and I would marry and save. I'd maybe buy my own drone for side work inspecting farm buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Does that give you enough time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Five years is enough to get qualified, get married and get a bit saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe fifteen hundred on a drone. Farmers round here pay for roof and crop surveys. A drone of my own would pay for itself in a year.

say: I'd say there's **time** to get ready, so let's be smart.
I'd tell people to **learn new tools** and stay flexible.
think: I think I'd have **drone skills** before robots arrive in 2034.
I think I'd **be okay**, as long as I keep learning and saving.
do: I'd do a **robotics course** part-time after qualifying.
I'd buy a **fifteen-hundred** drone for farm survey side work.
S3.quote: Farmers round here pay for roof and crop surveys. A drone of my own would pay for itself in a year.
fieldNote: Five years gives her time to **qualify, marry and save**.

steps.text: Take a part-time robotics course after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get it right. I'd tell people to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. I'd be experienced, with drone and robot skills, by 2039. The grid will still need building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, specialise in drones and robots, and grow the drone side business. Jonas and I would marry and start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 39 when robots arrive. How do you picture that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture myself leading a crew that's half robots, half people, with kids at the village school. And a drone business on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the people who don't adapt get left behind. And whether the company keeps us or hires outsiders.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to get it right.
I'd tell people to **start learning** now.
think: I think I'd have **drone and robot** skills by 2039, with the grid still growing.
do: I'd specialise in **drones and robots** after qualifying.
I'd grow the **drone side business** and start a family.
S4.quote: I picture myself leading a crew that's half robots, half people, with kids at the village school.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan **career and family** together, so calm fits.
Her worry shifts to **colleagues** who don't adapt.
She worries the company might **hire outsiders** instead of training crews.

steps.text: Specialise in drones and robot supervision after qualifying
Grow the farm drone survey business
Marry Jonas and start a family within a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be barely qualified, with two weeks saved and a wedding to plan. What would help is companies training their own people early, and tax breaks for firms that do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about women on crews. There's only a handful of women on transmission crews, and we have to prove ourselves twice. If cuts come, I'd want to be sure it's on skill, not who fits in.

headlineQuote: There's only a handful of women on transmission crews, and we have to prove ourselves twice.
portrait: Zoe is an **apprentice** on a travelling transmission crew, staying in motels four nights a week.
She lives with her boyfriend Jonas on his family's farm and has **two weeks** saved.
She uses **AI daily** and flies the company drone, aiming for inspection and robot work.
She's **traditional**, favouring company training and tax breaks over government support.
She's calm in Steady Disruption and AGI by 2036, but **anxious** under AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as she'd be **barely qualified** with a wedding to plan.
